newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori set for meeting with Hashimoto.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori set for meeting with Hashimoto.

text.p: Peruvian police stepped up pressure on Thursday on Marxist hostage-takers as President Alberto Fujimori prepared to travel to Canada for a crucial summit with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

Police repeatedly blasted broadcasts of martial music, sirens and the roar of aircraft at the Japanese ambassador's home where roughly 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels held 72 VIP hostages for the 44th day.

They also flew a helicopter and a twin-engine military plane over the site on several occasions, and sent an armoured personnel carrier rumbling close by, as part of their campaign to wear down the rebels' resolve.
With tensions high at the siege, President Alberto Fujimori prepared to leave for talks with Hashimoto in Canada over how to resolve the deadlocked crisis.
Fujimori was due to fly from Lima to Toronto in the presidential jet around midnight local time (0500 GMT), accompanied by journalists and officials.
According to senior government sources, the Peruvian president will then travel to Washington on Sunday for a meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton the following day.
Washington did not, however, confirm that version.

The Peruvian sources, all speaking on condition of anonymity, insisted Fujimori would not apologise to Hashimoto for the provocative police tactics at the siege site, which have worried Tokyo, or seek his approval for a military assault.
They said in his meeting with Clinton, Fujimori planned to thank him for Washington's strong backing during the crisis.
Hashimoto said on Thursday the weekend summit would confirm Tokyo and Lima's joint strategy of not "caving in to terrorism."
But he is likely to temper that tough talk with a plea that Lima avoid steps that could prompt the rebels to harm their hostages, who include two dozen Japanese, officials in Tokyo said.
"The meeting is not meddling with the Peruvian government, but is a discussion," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said.

Fujimori, who met for the first time with familes of the hostages at Government Palace on Thursday, has not commented publicly on Saturday's meeting. But his chief crisis negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, described it as a joint evaluation of "strategy set out to reach a solution."
Palermo told a news conference the meeting also "looks to make possible the carrying out of operative aspects" to end the crisis.
Outside the residence, police resumed their war of nerves in the early hours of Thursday by turning on their music for the first time during sleeping hours.
The half-hour recording of martial music, with aircraft in the background, created the impression helicopters and planes were approaching the fortified compound, witnesses said.

In the most provocative action yet, scores of policemen took part in a massive show of force in front of the compound Monday, driving past in an armoured convoy to the tune of the marching music. Some made obscene gestures, provoking a burst of gunfire from the rebels which narrowly missed policemen aboard one vehicle.
Hashimoto has called several times this week for Fujimori to exercise caution in the deployment of police at the site to prevent "accidents or incidents."
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said his country was chosen to host Hashimoto's meeting with Fujimori because of its mediating role in the crisis which has been accepted by both sides.

Canada's ambassador to Peru, Anthony Vincent, and Roman Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani -- who have been accepted by both sides to sit on a committee overseeing eventual peace talks -- will also travel with Fujimori.
Efforts to start talks with the MRTA guerrillas have stalled over their main demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, which Fujimori has refused to discuss.

The MRTA rebels originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed the residence Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception. They released most of the captives but kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, top government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and the Japanese.
